title: Managing a Python Installation
section: The Golden Rule of Python Environments
text:
The Golden Rule of Python Environments
When you want to install a package for Python (like pandas), many guides often tell you to open the terminal and type pip install pandas. Do not do this.
Operating systems like MacOS and Linux rely on a hidden, system-level Python installation to run core operating system background tasks. If you use global pip to install or upgrade packages, you risk overwriting the dependencies your operating system relies on. This leads to a broken OS, or at best, conflicting dependencies between your own projects (often called “Dependency Hell”).
Preventing Dependecy Hell: Every project must live in its own isolated “Virtual Environment.”
This is one of the downsides to Python, in order to prevent dependency conflicts you need to manage what amounts to different Python installations. Fortunately, there are solutions that make this less tedious and prone to complication.

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
uv
Historically, managing Python safely required juggling several different tools (pyenv for Python versions, venv for environments, pip for packages, and pipx for global apps).
There are multiple solutions to managing different Python installations (Conda/Miniconda are very popular), a recent one is uv. This replaces all of the traditional tools with a single tool. It operates entirely in user-space, meaning it requires no administrator privileges and generally can be installed without friction on computers that you do not have full control over.

1. Installing uv
Open your terminal and run the official standalone installer:
# On macOS/Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# On Windows
powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | more"


qua2. Installing Python Versions
You do not need to download Python from the official website. uv will download and isolate whatever version of Python you need for a project.
For example, if you need a Python version of 3.12 as a requirement:
# Install the latest version of Python 3.12
uv python install 3.12


3. Creating a Project
When creating a new project, uv makes environment isolation automatic.
# Create a new project directory
mkdir data_analysis_project
cd data_analysis_project

# Initialize the project structure
uv init

# Add a package (this automatically creates the virtual environment!)
uv add pandas matplotlib
Notice that we never had to manually “activate” an environment. By using uv add, the tool automatically handles the creation and linkage of the isolated environment.


4. Running Your Code
To run a script using the isolated environment, simply prefix your command with uv run.
# Runs script.py using the isolated pandas/matplotlib installation
uv run script.py

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
Installing Global Tools
Sometimes you need to install a Python application that you want to use everywhere, not just in one project. A good example is something like Jupyter Lab.
Installing an application into a specific project’s virtual environment is tedious, but installing them globally via pip breaks the Golden Rule.
The solution is an isolated tool runner.
# Install Jupyter Lab in its own isolated global environment
uv tool install jupyterlab

# You can now launch Jupyter from anywhere on your computer
jupyter lab
If you are working on a legacy system without uv, the traditional equivalent of this command is pipx install jupyterlab.

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
Working with Older Codebases
While uv is the modern standard, you will inevitably encounter older codebases or tutorials that use the standard library tools. Adjusting them to use uv is straightforward.
If a repository contains a requirements.txt file, the traditional setup workflow looks like this:

Create the Environment:

python3 -m venv .venv

Activate the Environment: (You must do this every time you open a new terminal)

# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate

# Windows
.venv\Scripts\activate

Install the Dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Deactivate:

deactivate

title: Managing a Python Installation
text:
Recap
Need a library for a script? (e.g., numpy, pandas) -> Use uv add or a local venv.
Need a standalone app? (e.g., jupyter) -> Use uv tool install or pipx.
Never use: pip install [package] outside of an active virtual environment.

title: 5: Functions
text:
We have used prebuilt functions repeatedly in this course (like print or input) and now we will look at building our own.
A function is a group of statements within a program that performs a specific task. This collection of statements is attached to a name, and the name can be used to perform those statements repeatedly without having to duplicate the underlying code.
This idea of code reuse is a primary benefit of functions. We get to write the code once then call it as many times as needed. This appreciably simplifies our codebase as it reduces duplicate code and this results in superior testing and debugged as we only need to test and debug just a single block of code, the function itself.


Function naming rules are very similar to those of variables:

Cannot use keywords as a function name
Cannot contain spaces
First character must be a letter or underscore
All other characters must be a letter, number or underscore
Uppercase and lowercase characters are distinct

And like variables, the function name should be descriptive of the task carried out by the function.




Defining a function:
def function_name(parameter_1,parameter_2, ...):
    statement_1
    statement_2
    ...

The function header is the first line of the function and includes the keyword def and the name of the function. This is followed by parentheses where the (optional) parameters needed by the function are placed and then ended with a colon.
Inside the function we have the statement or statements that you want the function to perform. Note that the statements inside the function must be indented.



To use a function, we call it by invoking its name.

def add(x,y):
    print(x + y)

add(2,3)

5


The simple function add above takes in two parameters, x and y then prints their summed value. A parameter is a variable that is assigned the value of an argument when the function is called. We call the function with specific values for the parameters, arguments, in this case 2 and 3 using the notation add(2,3). Note that the function assigns the parameter values in order of the arguments that are passed in. 2 is the first argument, so it is assigned to x and 3 is the second argument so it is assigned to y.
Functions can take in multiple arguments, a single argument or none at all. How many parameters are needed for a function is dependent on its construction.



The function we just saw does not return any data back out of the function, it simply prints a value to the terminal. We call this type of function that executes the statements it contains and then ends a void function.
In contrast, a value-returning function executes its statements and then returns some value back to the point of the program that called it. The input and int functions are example of value-returning functions that you have used.
To return a value from a function, you need only use the return keyword.

def add(x,y):
    return x + y

result = add(2,3)
print(result)

5


We can see in the modified version of our add function that we now return the sum of the values instead of printing to the terminal. This returned value is stored in the result variable and then this variable is printed to the terminal. Note that we do not need to tell Python what type of value is being returned unlike in some other programming languages. The return keyword only specifics to send that value back, there is no check to see what type of value it actually is.


We can return multiple values by separating the values by commas.

def add(x,y):
    return x + y, x, y

result = add(2,3)
print(result)

(5, 2, 3)


Our add function now returns the sum, then the value associated with parameter x and finally the value associated with parameter y. Note that the values are returned in the order they are specified. Also note that the variable result is now a tuple containing three objects, which is what we would expect since we returned three individual values.
We can assign these values immediately using the convention for multiple assignment:

def add(x,y):
    return x + y, x, y

result, x, y = add(2,3)
print(result)
print(x)
print(y)

5
2
3


If you choose to do multiple assignment from a function call, you will need exactly as many variables as there are returned values.



You can use the pass keyword to create empty functions. This keyword is ignored by the Python interpreter and this can be helpful when designing a program.

def a_function():
    pass





Changes made to a parameter value within the function do not affect the argument. This is known as pass by value and it provides a way for unidirectional communication between one function and another function.

def function_1():
    value = 5
    print(f'The value is {value}')
    function_2(value)
    print(f'The value is {value}')

def function_2(x):
    print(f'The value is {x}')
    x = 0
    print(f'The value is now {x}')

Note that in this example the value in the first function is passed to the second function, but the change is not reflected in the first function. The second function gets a copy of data in the first value and not the actual variable itself.


A keyword argument is an argument that specifies which parameter the value should be passed to.
function_name(parameter=value)
Note that the position when calling the function is not relevant. It is also possible to mix keyword arguments and positional arguments when calling a function but all positional arguments must appear first.
Keyword arguments are often used to provide a default argument for a parameter. A default argument is a value that will be there by default unless explicitly overwritten when the function is called.
In the following example we can omit passing a value into the tax rate parameter because a default argument is provided. We are still free to overwrite it whenever we need.

def show_tax(price, tax_rate=0.08):
    tax = price * tax_rate
    print(f'The tax is {tax}.')

show_tax(10)

show_tax(10,tax_rate=0.10)

The tax is 0.8.
The tax is 1.0.






In Python, scope determines the visibility and lifetime of a variable. That is, scope is the part of a program in which a variable may be accessed.
Python follows the LEGB rule, which defines the order in which the interpreter searches for a variable name.

Local
Enclosing
Global
Built-in



A local variable is variable that is assigned a value inside a function. It belongs to the function in which it was created.
Only statements inside that function can access it, an error will occur if another function tries to access the variable. The scope of a local variable is the function where it was created and any local variables are destroyed when their associated function ends.
A local variable cannot be accessed by statements inside its function which precede its creation. You also cannot access a local variable after the function ends as it no longer exists.
Note that because the scope of a local variable is constrained to its associated function, different functions may have local variables with the same name. Each function does not see the other function’s local variables, so there is no ambiguity to the Python interpreter.
def my_func():
    x = 10  # Local scope
    print(x)

my_func()
# print(x)  # Throws NameError: name 'x' is not defined
Notice how in the example below that despite having the same name, the variables in function 1 and function 2 are different.

x = 10

def function_1():
        x = 4
        print(x)

def function_2():
        print(x)

function_1()
function_2()

4
10





Enclosing (or nonlocal) scope occurs in nested functions. It represents the scope of the outer (enclosing) function from the perspective of the inner function.
By default, an inner function can read variables in the enclosing scope, but attempting to modify them will create a new local variable in the inner function instead. You must use the nonlocal keyword if you intend to mutate an enclosing variable.
However, heavy use of nested functions and nonlocal state can make code difficult to debug and reason about.

def outer_function():
    message = "Hello"  # Enclosing scope
    
    def inner_function():
        nonlocal message
        message = "Hi"  # Modifies the enclosing variable
        
    inner_function()
    print(message)  # Outputs: Hi




Global scope comprises variables defined at the top level of a script, module, or notebook cell. They are accessible anywhere within that specific module. A global variable is created by assignment statement written outside all the functions.
Global variables can be accessed by any statement in the program file, including from within a function. If a function needs to assign a value to the global variable, the global variable must be redeclared within the function.

counter = 0  # Global scope

def increment():
    global counter
    counter += 1

Global variables should generally be avoided as they make debugging difficult. Many portions of the program can change the value of a global variable and as a program becomes larger, finding which location is changing the variable becomes difficult.



Built-in scope is the widest scope. It contains all of Python’s built-in objects, functions, and exceptions (things like print(), len(), list, int, etc.). This scope is automatically loaded whenever you run Python.
Python allows you to reuse built-in names for your own variables like naming a variable list = [1, 2, 3]. This is called shadowing.
sum = 10
a_list = [1,2,3]

print(sum(a_list)) # TypeError: 'int' object is not callable
Once you shadow a built-in name, you lose access to the original built-in function within that scope, which leads to subtle, frustrating bugs later. Always avoid using Python keywords or built-in function names as variable identifiers.




We can differentiate variables that may appear to be the same (by having the same value) using the id() function. The id() function returns a unique identifier, the object’s memory address.

If two variables are stored at the same memory address, they must refer to the same data.
If two variables are stored at different memory addresses, then while they might refer to the same value, they do not refer to the same physical data and so are different to Python.


var1 = 5
var2 = 5

print(f'Var 1 = {id(var1)} \t Var 2 = {id(var2)}')

Var 1 = 4355928160   Var 2 = 4355928160



var1 = 5
var2 = var1

print(f'Var 1 = {id(var1)} \t Var 2 = {id(var2)}')

Var 1 = 4355928160   Var 2 = 4355928160

title: 2: Variables Arithmetic Basic I/O
text:
A variable is a name that represents a value stored in memory. Variables are used to access and manipulate data stored in these memory locations.


An assignment is the process that is used to create a variable and make it reference data (or reference different data if the variable already exists).
The general format of an assignment statement is:

The general format for assignment is:
variable_name = expression

For example:

mass = 50

This sets the variable mass to the value 50.
Be careful not to confuse the assignment operator = with the equals sign. In Python, this symbol is used for assignment. When we reach conditional statements in the future, we will see that the equality operator (which asks the questions are two objects equal) is the double equals sign ==.
Note that in our examples, the variable receiving the value is always on the left side. This is a general rule in Python, the variable that takes on the value must be on the left.
We also can only use a variable if there is a value actually assigned to it.
number = 
The code above here is broken, as the variable named number is not assigned to anything. This will cause a syntax error.


You can also assign values to multiple variables in a single statement. This is known as multiple assignment.
The following code blocks are functionally equivalent:

x, y, z = 0, 1, 2


x = 0
y = 1
z = 2





The purpose of data types is to categorize the value located in memory.
The major types in Python are: - int for integer - float for a real number - str for sequences of characters (these can be any kind of symbol from letters to numbers to punctuation and more) - bool for Boolean values (True or False)
Some operations behave differently depending on the data type (or may not even be defined at all). For example, the + operator performs standard addition when used on ints and floats but instead performs concatenation when used with two strs.



This example demonstrates the idea of copying by value.

x = 7
y = x
x = 10
print(y)

7



y gets the value of x at the time of assignment
Changing x later does not change y
y still prints 7

For simple data types (numbers, strings, Booleans), assignment behaves like copying a value.
With more complex data types (like lists which will be introduced soon), variables behave differently.
The assignment shares access to the same data. The variable names point to a location that holds a single instance of the data. If you change the data through one variable, it will be reflected to all the other variables that point at the same underlying data.
For simple types (int, float, str, bool) assignment copies the value.
For complex types (lists and many others) assignment shares access to the same data.



Python has a set of rules for naming variables. Most of these if ignored will result in a syntax error.

Variable name cannot be a Python keyword
Variable name cannot contain spaces
First character must be a letter or an underscore
After first character may use letters, digits, or underscores
Variable names are case sensitive

In general, a variable’s name should reflect its use. This makes finding and fixing problems in your code much easier. Note that it is common for certain variables to have very simple names (i, j, k, etc.) when they are used for certain common operations. When starting out, you may want to use a more descriptive name to help your understanding.



We know that variables can reference different values while program is running. This is another way of saying we can reassign variables.
Howver, Python does not check to see if your variable’s type is valid for what you are trying to do (this differs from some other programming languages). If you reassign a variable to a different type, you could break code that was previously working.
Also, in Python, you do not need to worry about deleting variables after they have been used (like some other programming languages). Values that are no longer referenced by variables are automatically removed by Python’s garbage collector.



Casting is the process of converting on type of data to another. In Python this is accomplished by a set of functions that is built directly into the language.









Function
Description
Example
Output




int()
Converts to an integer. Truncates floats towards zero.
int(3.8)int(“4”)
34


float()
Converts to a floating-point number.
float(3)float(“3.14”)
33.14


str()
Converts almost any object into its string representation.
str(100)
“100”


bool()
Converts to a boolean (True or False).
bool(1)bool(““)
TrueFalse



There are certain restrictions on casting in Python that will cause a runtime error if ignored. - Non-Numeric Strings to Numeric Types - Attempting to cast a string that does not look like a number will raise a ValueError. - int(“apple”) - Casting Float-like Strings to Integers - Python cannot directly cast a string containing a decimal point straight into an integer. - score = int(“98.6”)



A magic number is an unexplained numeric value that appears in a program’s code.
For example:
amount = balance * 0.065
The value 0.065 is not specified as to what it actually is. It could be an interest rate, or a fee percentage, or many other possible things. Only the person who wrote the code knows for sure (assuming they remember).
If a magic number is used in many places in a program it can take substantial effort to find and change the number in each location. You take the risk of making a mistake each type you type the magic number the program’s code. This can be the source of difficult to find and frustrating errors.


Rather than using magic numbers, you should used a variable whose purpose is to represent the value. This variable is not intended to be changed during the program and so is called a constant. In practice, Python will allow you to change the value, so it is important to remember that this variable is supposed to be static. The common convention in Python is to use all caps to indicate a constant variable.

INTEREST_RATE = 0.051





None is a special Python value that represents no value assigned yet. Note that None is a value (not an error). Its data type is a unique NoneType.
None is used as a placeholder when a value is unknown or not available.
None is not the same as: - 0 (a number) - “” (an empty string) - False (a Boolean)
We use None to: - Initialize a variable before it has a real value - Represent missing or unknown information - Indicate that a result has not been computed yet
Rule to remember: Do not perform math or string operations on None. - Any of these operations causes an error.

An assignment is the process that is used to create a variable and make it reference data (or reference different data if the variable already exists).
The general format of an assignment statement is:

The general format for assignment is:
variable_name = expression

For example:

mass = 50

This sets the variable mass to the value 50.
Be careful not to confuse the assignment operator = with the equals sign. In Python, this symbol is used for assignment. When we reach conditional statements in the future, we will see that the equality operator (which asks the questions are two objects equal) is the double equals sign ==.
Note that in our examples, the variable receiving the value is always on the left side. This is a general rule in Python, the variable that takes on the value must be on the left.
We also can only use a variable if there is a value actually assigned to it.
number = 
The code above here is broken, as the variable named number is not assigned to anything. This will cause a syntax error.


You can also assign values to multiple variables in a single statement. This is known as multiple assignment.
The following code blocks are functionally equivalent:

x, y, z = 0, 1, 2


x = 0
y = 1
z = 2

title: 2: Variables Arithmetic Basic I/O
text:
The purpose of data types is to categorize the value located in memory.
The major types in Python are: - int for integer - float for a real number - str for sequences of characters (these can be any kind of symbol from letters to numbers to punctuation and more) - bool for Boolean values (True or False)
Some operations behave differently depending on the data type (or may not even be defined at all). For example, the + operator performs standard addition when used on ints and floats but instead performs concatenation when used with two strs.

title: 2: Variables Arithmetic Basic I/O
text:
This example demonstrates the idea of copying by value.

x = 7
y = x
x = 10
print(y)

7



y gets the value of x at the time of assignment
Changing x later does not change y
y still prints 7

For simple data types (numbers, strings, Booleans), assignment behaves like copying a value.
With more complex data types (like lists which will be introduced soon), variables behave differently.
The assignment shares access to the same data. The variable names point to a location that holds a single instance of the data. If you change the data through one variable, it will be reflected to all the other variables that point at the same underlying data.
For simple types (int, float, str, bool) assignment copies the value.
For complex types (lists and many others) assignment shares access to the same data.

text:
The Print Function
We have already seen the print function in the Hello World example. The print function will be one of the most commonly used functions throughout this course. It is extremely useful when trying to debug code, as you can see the contents of variables as your program progresses through its instructions.

Program Execution Order
In general, statements execute in the order that they appear. Specifically, the go from top (first) to bottom (last). In the future we will see ways of repeating or skipping sections of code.
The output of the following example is ‘one’ then ‘two’ then ‘three’.

print('one')
print('two')
print('three')

one
two
three




Displaying Multiple Items with the Print Function
Python allows one to display multiple items with a single call to print. - Items are separated by commas when passed as arguments. - Arguments displayed in the order they are passed to the function. - Items are automatically separated by a space when displayed on screen.

print('one', 'two', 'three')

one two three


Based off the previous examples we can see that successive print statements place their value(s) on different lines. This is because the print function puts a newline character at the end of printed data. We can change this default newline to a value of our choice using the special argument end.
The following example changes the default newline to a space.

print('one',end=' ')
print('two',end=' ')
print('three',end=' ')

one two three 


Similarly, for multiple items displayed on the same line, we can use the separator argument sep to change the default space to something else.
The following example changes the default space to a dash.

print('one', 'two', 'three',sep='-')

one-two-three


Both of these options can be useful to help format printed values to make reading their output easier.


Newlines and Tabs
Certain special characters are preceded by a backslash \.
These characters are treated as commands inside a string.
To create a newline, we use the character \n.
Note the extra new line in the following example.

print('Hello world\n')
print('Hello world')

Hello world

Hello world


To create a tab, we use \t.
Note the increased whitespace (the tab character) between the words Hello and world.

print('Hello\tworld')

Hello   world


We can also see that there is no additional space here in the string Hello\tworld and yet the tab is still correctly placed. If we included space between the tab and the other parts of the string like:

print('Hello \t world')

Hello    world


We see that there is additional space in the printed output. This is an important feature of printing strings in that anything inside the string is printed exactly as it is written. By adding the spaces to make things easier for us to read inside the string, we altered the output.

title: 2: Variables Arithmetic Basic I/O
text:
The Input Function
Many programs need to read input from the user. While many kinds of data can be used as input, we will largely be dealing with the simple input function and working with text data. More complicated kinds of input tend to require more effort to both read and process, so we will avoid these in an introductory course.
The input function displays an optional prompt and then reads input from the keyboard.

variable_name = input("Your Prompt Here")

Note that the input function always returns the data as a string.
The prompt is typically a string instructing user to enter a value.
The input function also does not automatically display a space after the prompt.
For example:
name = input("What is your name?  ")
The above does the following:

Displays the string ‘What is your name?’
Reads input, as a string, from the keyboard
Assigns the string that was read from the keyboard to the name variable


Reading Numbers with the Input Function
Since the input function always returns a string, if we want to use the input as a number in calculations we will need to cast the string to the appropriate numerical type.
number = int(input('Enter a number: '))
The above does the following:

Displays the string ‘Enter a number:’
Reads input, as a string, from the keyboard
Converts the input to an int
Assigns the resulting int to the number variable

Converting Math Formulas into Python
In Python, an operator is required for any mathematical operation. Standard mathematical notation like xy which is implicitly understood that x and y are multiplied together is not allowed in Python. Any mathematical operation needs to be explicitly defined using operators.
In general, converting math formulas into Python tends to require adding multiplication operators and the insertion of parentheses.


Mixed-Type Expressions and Automatic Type Conversion
The data type resulting from mathematical operations depends on the type of operands. - Two int operands results in another int - Two float operands results in another float - One int operands and one float operand results in a float

text:
This course is about problem solving using computers.
Having a computer solve a problem requires the creation of a set of instructions, a program .

The process of creating these instructions is programming .

Problem solving means the ability to formulate problems, think creatively about solutions, and express a solution clearly and accurately.
The process of learning to program is an excellent opportunity to practice problem solving skills.

title: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment
text:
Syntax Errors
Python can only execute a program if the program is syntactically correct ; otherwise, the process fails and returns an error message.  Syntax refers to the structure of a program and the rules about that structure. For example, in English, a sentence must begin with a capital letter and end with a period. If there is a single syntax error anywhere in your program, Python will display an error message and quit. You will not be able to complete the execution of your program. During the first few weeks of your programming career, you will probably spend a lot of time tracking down syntax errors. However, as you gain experience, you will make fewer errors, and you will also be able to find your errors faster.
crumbs: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment

title: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment
text:
Runtime Errors
The second type of error is a runtime error, so called because the error does not appear until you run the program. These errors are also called exceptions because they usually indicate that something exceptional (and bad) has happened. Runtime errors are rare in the simple programs you will see in the first few chapters, so it might be a while before you encounter one.
crumbs: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment

title: 1: Course Introduction and the Python Environment
text:
Semantic Errors
If there is a semantic error in your program, it will run successfully in the sense that the computer will not generate any error messages. However, your program will not do the right thing. It will do something else. Specifically, it will do exactly what you told it to do.

The problem is that the program you wrote is not the program you wanted to write. The meaning of the program (its semantics) is wrong.
Identifying semantic errors can be tricky because it requires you to work backward by looking at the output of the program and trying to figure out what it is doing.
